title: The Turing jump and stronger halting problems

based_on.title: Computability theory
based_on.pages: Version 2024-02-25; §15.2, pp.64–65 (Definition 15.9, Theorem 15.10, Exercises 15.11–12), and §16.1, p.67 (Proposition 16.4)

summary: Every oracle has a strictly stronger halting problem, complete for the sets it can recognize.
abstract: Suppose a program can ask whether a number belongs to a fixed set. Those answers still cannot let it decide, for every program using that same set, whether that program halts on its own code. Treating these halting questions as a new membership problem gives the Turing jump, which is strictly harder than the original oracle. Every set recognizable with that oracle reduces to its jump by an ordinary computable translation of inputs, and translations between jumps capture exactly when one original oracle can decide membership in another. The jump therefore acts on degrees, the classes of membership problems that can decide one another, and finite iteration gives a strictly increasing chain above every degree. For an empty or decidable oracle, an explicit change of program codes recovers the ordinary halting problem.
